contentMarkdown:
Everyone hits this sooner or later: a single invoice buried in a 40-page bank statement, your resume stuck inside a full portfolio, or one chapter you need out of a course pack. Splitting a PDF — pulling the pages you need into a fresh file — takes under a minute, and it's free.

## Method 1: the free online splitter (fastest)

No software to install, no account to create. Your browser does the whole job, and the file never leaves your device.

1. Open the [free Split PDF tool](/tools/split-pdf).
2. Drop in your PDF.
3. Choose how to split it:
   - **Page ranges** — type what you want, like `1-3, 5, 8-10`, and get exactly those pages as a new PDF.
   - **Every N pages** — set N to 5 and a 23-page PDF becomes separate files of 5, 5, 5, 5, and 3 pages.
   - **Pick pages** — tick pages visually in a preview grid.
4. Download your new PDF.

This is the method to use when you need *multiple* splits or odd page combinations. Splitting several invoices out of one monthly statement, for example, takes one pass with page ranges instead of repeating the whole process for each invoice.

## Method 2: your computer's built-in tools

If you just need to pull one page range out and don't want a website, your OS already has it covered.

**Mac (Preview):** open the PDF, choose **File → Print**, set the page range in the Pages section, then click the **PDF** button at the bottom-left and choose **Save as PDF**. To extract non-adjacent pages, select their thumbnails in the sidebar first.

**Windows:** open the PDF in Edge or Chrome, press **Ctrl+P**, set the destination to **Microsoft Print to PDF**, and enter your pages under "Pages" (e.g. `5-8`). Windows can't split into equal parts this way — for that, use the online splitter above.

## Method 3: on your phone

The online splitter works directly in your mobile browser: open it in Safari or Chrome, pick the PDF from your files, and save the result. No app to install.

**iPhone shortcut:** open the PDF, tap Share → **Print**, then pinch outward on the print preview to open it as a PDF and tap **Save to Files**. It's quick for a single page range but clumsy for anything complex.

## Which method should you use?

- **One page range, one file:** your built-in print-to-PDF is fine.
- **Multiple splits, equal parts, or odd combinations:** the [Split PDF tool](/tools/split-pdf) is faster and less error-prone.
- **Merging instead of splitting:** that's the reverse job — combining several files into one. Use the [free Merge PDF tool](/tools/merge-pdf).
- **Splitting to shrink what you send:** if you're pulling one chapter out of a manual to email it, split first, then run the smaller file through the [free compress PDF tool](/tools/compress-pdf). A smaller source makes a smaller output — and nobody waits on a 40-page attachment when they only need six pages.

## The honest limits

- **Password-protected PDFs can't be split until unlocked.** If a file asks for a password, you'll need it first — and only unlock documents you own or have the right to open.
- **Scanned PDFs stay scans.** Splitting copies pages exactly as they are, so a scan remains a scan (no selectable text appears out of thin air). Pages are copied at full fidelity — images keep their resolution and text stays selectable if it was selectable before.
- **Very large files take a moment.** The work happens on your device, so a 500-page PDF processes as fast as your phone or laptop can handle it. Give it a few seconds.
- **Keep the original.** Split copies are cheap to make, but you can't un-split — hang on to the source file in case you need different pages later.
